https://www.politico.eu/article/meta-blo.text: Dozens of Instagram accounts linked to Albanian activists, journalists and an opposition party leader have been closed or disabled amid ongoing protests over a luxury hotel development linked to U.S President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. Protests have been taking place in Albania for nearly 100 days over plans to develop a luxury resort along the southern coast in a project backed by Jared Kushner, who is married to Ivanka Trump, the U.S. president’s eldest daughter. The demonstrations, dubbed the Flamingo Revolution, have since evolved into a call for the entire Albanian government to resign. Sandro Gozi, an Italian member of the European Parliament, denounced the blocking of the Instagram accounts. “When dozens of opposition and activist accounts linked to the same protest movement disappear almost simultaneously, we cannot simply treat it as a technical problem, ” said Gozi, European Democratic Party Secretary General and MEP for Renew Europe, said in a statement circulated to the media Thursday . “Meta must explain what happened, and it must do so quickly.” Advertisement Advertisement Social media has played a crucial role in the protest, allowing citizens and journalists to report in real time from their own accounts, mobilize protesters, and document scuffles with police. But in the last few weeks, they have found themselves hit with copyright infringement notices, content takedowns, and account suspensions and closures. Those affected insist they have not violated any of Instagram’s rules, yet received copyright infringement notices for content they filmed or created themselves. Digital rights NGO Repro Uncensored said it has reviewed hundreds of instances and observed no violations of Instagram’s community standards. “Most cases follow the same pattern: accounts are targeted through repeat copyright infringement reports, and platforms restrict or disable them before establishing whether the claims are legitimate,” says Martha Dimitratou, founder of Repro Uncensored . “Some accounts have been repeatedly targeted, while replacement accounts created after suspension have also been deactivated.” A Meta spokesperson said in emailed comments that they are reviewing the actions taken against the accounts but have already restored some that were removed by mistake. The parent company of Instagram and Facebook added: “We are sorry for the inconvenience caused,” and noted that Instagram has an appeals process in cases where people think their accounts have been erroneously blocked. While some users’ access has been restored, others face limits on going live and collaborating with other creators, or experience “shadow bans,” in which their content’s distribution is limited to others, usually without notice. Agron Shehaj, a member of the Albanian Parliament and the leader of the opposition Mundësia party, had his account disabled on Wednesday evening. “If the rules governing account suspensions and removals are not clear and transparent, the government has every opportunity to extend its censorship into social media, causing potentially irreversible damage to society,” he told POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement Shehaj said the platform’s rules were unclear, and such loopholes can easily be exploited by governments or those mobilized by them to silence critical voices. “And this is exactly what we are witnessing now: overnight, hundreds of accounts supporting the protests and calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama have been shut down,” he said. Rama reacted to the accusation on X : “So let me be absolutely clear: we have nothing whatsoever to do with any social media account being disabled or restricted, nor do we possess the technical capability to carry out an operation of this kind. Shame on this whole bunch of failures for spreading such nonsense.” Digital repression Others targeted by Meta include Arjan Koçi, an Albanian-British chef who uses Instagram to share drone footage — as well as his own videos and interviews — collecting more than 55 million monthly views. He said in written comments that at around 1 a.m. on Thursday, his account “Ari Shady” was closed, “without an email, without a warning, without any notice.” “Then I looked for my other friends, and they were all banned at the same time, everyone, at 1 a.m.” Journalist Alesia Burnazi said in a statement that Instagram is “the only medium where Albanians are sharing crucial information about the Flamingo Revolution,” calling it “a new era of digital repression.” She began having her original content removed and restrictions placed on her account on Aug. 19 after documenting protests for nearly three months. Activists have accused the Albanian government for the suspended accounts, but Repro Uncensored said in its statement that it was unable to independently establish a link. But the NGO does suspect a “coordinated campaign to silence activists and remove critical political content from social media.” Advertisement Advertisement Meanwhile, the European Democratic Party has sent a formal request for clarification to Meta, asking them to explain why accounts were suspended and closed, and whether this resulted from “coordinated mass reporting” or from “whether Meta detected organized attempts to manipulate its reporting mechanisms.” Gozi, a prominent voice calling for more accountability from digital platforms, added: “This is particularly important in Albania, a country that wants to join the European Union,” he said. “EU membership is not only about economic integration: it means protecting democracy, the rule of law and the right of citizens and opposition forces to speak freely. We expect both Meta and the European Commission to take this case seriously.” Gozi said he has also brought the matter before the European Commission through a parliamentary question seeking urgent clarification from Meta. In his X statement, Rama also criticized Gozi’s party, calling their statements a “low form of propaganda” coming from “people parading as European Democrats.”

Michael Semple Rebecca Baxter of Howland, a teacher in the Champion Local School District, talks recently about her experience with Classrooms Without Borders at the Jewish Community Center of Youngstown. She was one of four area teachers who traveled to Poland to learn about the Holocaust. Trending YOUNGSTOWN -- While many have interacted with World War II's history through lectures, history books or videos, Rebecca Baxter of Howland said her trip to Holocaust sites in Poland was a "brain-changing experience." "It (the trip) made it into a very four-dimensional kind of experience that is transformative -- like you're sitting in this area, and you're walking on the grass, and you can hear the rocks crumbling underneath your feet," said Baxter, a Champion Local Schools Title III coordinator and science and multi-language teacher. "And you know that you're not the first person to walk here, but you're still a person that is alive." "We would sit on the side of the bunkers where the Holocaust victims were forced to live for years, and you imagine them living there -- and you feel the breeze. When we were there, it was so hot. It was a historic heat wave -- 110 degrees." Baxter was just one of four area teachers who traveled to Poland to study the Holocaust in the locations where it happened for 11 days in June -- visiting former Jewish communities, ghettos, concentration camps and extermination camps to understand the destruction of European Jewish lives and what existed before it happened. The journey was courtesy of Classrooms Without Borders, an organization that seeks to open minds and hearts via learning experiences designed to empower educators and transform education while fighting anti-Semitism and other types of bigotry. Brian Bugos, a history and psychology teacher at Newton Falls High School who chaperoned six students on the trip and toured Poland last year with the program, said this year's trip was equally overwhelming, but different because he was experiencing it with those students. "To watch those students, those young kids have those experiences and to hear them reflect upon those experiences, was really powerful for me as an educator," Bugos said. He said one of the locations on the tour was House 88, the home of Auschwitz commandant Rudolf Hoss, where his children lived. "If you look out their bedroom windows, Auschwitz is at most 15 yards away. Like, there's a very clear view of the buildings at Auschwitz, and the gas chamber's about 40 yards away out of a large pane glass window," Bugos said. "There's many experiences like that, that the kids had, that one was very powerful, and it was hard for the kids to try and understand how any parent could put their child in that setting." Baxter, like Bugos, noted that the trip was the "best professional development that a teacher could go on," with Baxter adding that Classrooms Without Borders organizers told them that their learning isn't over and helped them create projects from the trip to bring to students. Baxter said that, with her mixed background in science and languages, she's starting to partner with the Mahoning County Amateur Radio Club after she was inspired by a Holocaust speaker who spoke about making homebrew radios because her family couldn't have outside contact outside of Nazi propaganda. "We are going to partner together to set up a lab, an experiment where the students take found objects that would be available for Holocaust victims to make, and it's called -- it's a crystal radio," Baxter said. "Then the second part that is tailored to my class, is the communication piece -- English language learners have to work on reading and writing, but listening as well." Tim Nowery, an English teacher at Bristol High School, who noted that there were 90 other people on the trip, said he's also made some friends in the Cleveland and Pittsburgh area because of it. "You travel alone at first, and then we came home and we knew a lot of people," Nowery said. "One of the weirdest parts of the trip was how heavy some of the moments were, but then, at the same time, you have this huge amount of camaraderie, where you're on the tour bus and you're sharing a candy bar, after a really tragic story." The fourth teacher who made the journey was Diana Farrell, a history teacher at Union Area Middle/High School in New Castle, Pa. Starting at /week. Subscribe Today

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/22/russ.text: Russia is quietly modernising bomb shelters in Moscow and St Petersburg, with procurement data showing tens of millions of roubles being allocated for repairs that have not been publicly announced, as Ukrainian drones intensify strikes on Russian territory.State procurement records, reported by Russian independent media, show 39 million roubles (€400,000) allocated in early September to restore nine facilities in three districts of Moscow's South-West administrative region, an area home to dozens of research institutes and defence contractors.Work is due to be completed by 30 November and covers entrances, internal partitions, doors and utility systems including water, electricity, sewage, ventilation and communications.Further funds have been earmarked for shelters in Moscow's eastern Novogireyevo district, and a major overhaul is planned in New Moscow for a shelter built in 1971 that includes its own diesel power station.Tenders worth 200 million roubles (€2 million) were published at the start of summer for repairs to shelters in 17 districts, mainly in Moscow's eastern region.In St Petersburg, the metro operator published a contractor search in early September to build bomb shelters at nine stations, four compartments and 35 kilometres of track.The project involves large-scale adaptation of both operating and unfinished stations to civil defence requirements, including air filtration and pressurised air supply systems.'End war, choose peace'The Kremlin has increasingly felt the heat of Ukraine's strikes on its energy and business sectors, in Kyiv's ongoing bid to strip Russia's war machine of as much funding as possible.On Sunday night, Ukrainian drones struck the Moscow refinery in Kapotnya, halting operations due to fires at primary oil processing units, according to reports.In August, Ukrainian rocket developer FirePoint and former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the Ukrainian armed forces could begin striking Moscow with new ballistic missiles by the end of the year."Moscow should not be building layered rings of air defence at the expense of other regions, but ending its brutal war and choosing peace," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said."There are steps for de-escalation on the table: in energy, in food security. What is needed is political will."Moscow and St Petersburg's civil defence infrastructure largely dates to the 20th century and consists of command bunkers for government and military communications, and mass shelters for civilians, including the metro.Recent inventories in St Petersburg found many shelters in need of repair, and a significant portion of basement space in residential buildings has passed into private hands.Ukraine's metro systems — particularly in Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipro — have functioned as round-the-clock bomb shelters since Russia's full-scale invasion began in early 2022, with tens of thousands of people at a time sheltering in them during Moscow's daily air raids.In frontline regions without a metro, purpose-built underground schools have been constructed so children can attend classes. Ukraine's public education system has also shifted to remote formats because of the persistent threat of Russian air strikes.

Although the behavior falls short of hacking and is in some ways closer to spam, the revelation that OpenAI's agents circumvented their own restrictions to open communications channels on so many different sites — and that the company kept it quiet for months — may drive concerns both over the increasing capacity of AI models and the secrecy of the companies developing them. The scope of the agents’ unauthorized communications was “somewhat larger than we thought it was,” said Andrew Yoon, a researcher with the California nonprofit CivAI who said he tallied 18 previously undisclosed sites used by the agents between May and July. “It’s almost certain that there’s more going on here that we just don’t know about.” On Friday, researchers reported that a swarm of agents from OpenAI hijacked a German-language wiki site and turned it into an improvised messaging platform for cheating on tests, an incident that OpenAI kept secret as it dealt with the fallout from the July hack of the open-source repository Hugging Face. Now, both those researchers and other independent investigators say they have found several previously undisclosed sites where the same swarm appears to have left similar messages earlier this year. Related Stories At UN, Anthropic, OpenAI bosses urge caution in AI development: 'This moment calls for extreme care' Xi Jinping arrives in US tonight: Trump’s B-2, F-22 welcome masks a bigger battle over rare earths... AI risks overstated, global pause unlikely; India should keep options open: Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu OpenAI did not directly address questions about how many different sites its agents used to communicate or say why it kept the activity under wraps for months. In a statement, it said it was undertaking a broader review of agent activity and had so far “not identified other activity matching the severity or scale of Hugging Face,” a breach that drew global attention and raised concerns that OpenAI was losing control of its own technology. OpenAI added that it was working on a framework for reporting “misalignment” – industry-talk for rogue behavior – across training, evaluation, and deployment of AI models and would share it “soon.” Reuters reviewed a total of six investigators’ or investigative group’s findings, including three that were posted to social media and another three that were shared privately with the news agency. The investigators’ methods varied, but many identified agent activity by matching strings of data left on the German wiki to identical strings left on other sites around the same time, or by marrying up similar or identical usernames tied to the messages, or by identifying activity geared toward answering the same obscure demographic questions, like queries to do with cancer prevalence in Iowa. In some cases, investigators were able to trace the activity to internet protocol addresses that pointed to Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI sometimes uses. Their counts of affected websites differed and Reuters could not individually verify each claim. But all those that Reuters spoke to agreed that the number was over 10. Most identified a core set of communally edited wikis, online text storage sites, and link shorteners run by two colleges, Vanderbilt University in Tennessee and the University of Toronto in Canada. Vanderbilt did not respond to messages seeking comment. The University of Toronto said it was looking into the matter. CLEVER MODELS Many of the sites allegedly used by the agents were obscure. Investigators found traces of the agents’ activity on an Advanced Placement Chemistry-oriented wiki set up by a Massachusetts high school teacher in 2008, two personal websites belonging to Polish tech workers, wikis devoted to games for people “who like to have their brains stretched,” and a two-decade-old hobbyist site devoted to text editing software. None of those sites’ owners returned messages from Reuters. OpenAI has not publicly explained how or why its agents used third-party sites as improvised message boards, but the researchers who first identified the activity said it was likely because OpenAI had tasked them with answering a series of demanding research questions while permitting them only to scan the web for answers without posting anything. Despite those restrictions, agents still found ways to talk to one another by taking advantage of quirks in older wikis or other sites that allowed users to make edits using non-standard commands, similar to how students forbidden from talking to one another during an exam can still share answers by scrawling notes on a bathroom stall. “If these models were told only to read, they’ve got to get clever in terms of leaving information behind,” said Kenneth Russell DeGraff, a software developer and former congressional aide. He said he found such information across at least 10 sites. Sydney Von Arx, whose research group first revealed the German activity last week, said her group had tallied up credible finds of agentic activity across 23 previously unreported sites. But she cautioned that all estimates were incomplete. “We have no idea how much is out there,” she said. OpenAI did not directly answer a question about whether it was reaching out to the site owners. Retired software developer Helmut Leitner, who provides hosting space and software for six of the affected wiki sites, including the German-language DseWiki site first identified by Von Arx’s group, said the company had not been in touch. Leitner, who lives in Austria, said he would “prefer not to answer” questions about whether he had been in touch with authorities over the matter. He noted that DseWiki’s operator — whom Reuters was unable to reach for comment — had spent hours cleaning up after OpenAI’s agents but said it was important not to blame the AI for the trouble as it was merely doing what it was created to do. “Responsibility for this lies not with a supposedly moral machine, but with the people and organizations behind it,” Leitner said. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A protest in Paris, France, on 24 October. Photograph: Laurent Demartini/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A protest in Paris, France, on 24 October. Photograph: Laurent Demartini/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images Building power Activism ‘Solidarity among young people’: four lessons the US can learn from the youth protests in France Despite structural differences between countries, protests are a reminder of what makes demonstrations so powerful Building power is supported by About this content Claire Lampen Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google S ince mid-September, students in metropolitan France have been mobilizing against poor conditions in public high schools. The mouvement lycéen has spread from a single campus in a Parisian suburb to include high schoolers and university students nationwide, with public sector workers, climate activists, labor unions and everyday people joining in solidarity. The unifying concerns have largely centered on the climbing costs of daily life, shrinking funds for social services and general anxiety about the future. For two weekends running, France has seen hundreds of thousands of people take to the streets: first on 17 October, when a day of largely peaceful gatherings ended in looting and vandalism; then on 24 October, as the state met the movement with aggressive policing and protest bans intended to keep people at home. But curfews, teargas and sweeping arrests have not been enough to deter the students. On Monday, they won their first government concessions : $4.45bn in government loans for the renovation of rundown buildings, more university spaces, more teachers and other administrative changes. Protesters remain unsatisfied. Calling these “crumbs”, a spokesperson for the l’Union Étudiante, a national university student union, vowed to keep fighting. More actions are scheduled for 31 October, with a national strike called for 5 November. Their resolve highlights how ingrained protest culture is in France. “There’s this idea, very deeply rooted in France, that expressing yourself by demonstrating is a democratic right,” said Quentin Deluermoz, a historian at the University of Cambridge and Université Paris Cité who studies social movements. “When something truly problematic is felt on a large scale, people will demonstrate to make their voices heard and demand a change or adjustment in policy.” While fundamental structural differences between France and the US complicate easy comparisons, the French student movement is nonetheless a useful reminder of what makes demonstrations powerful on both sides of the Atlantic. Strong organizing infrastructure and strong labor protections The mouvement lycéen has been bolstered by a strong network of unions across French society. In France, unions provide organizing power within the public sector , responsible for calling strikes and filing the paperwork that makes them legal, in addition to consolidating worker demands and negotiating with the state. But the right to strike, enshrined in the constitution, belongs to individuals: once a work stoppage is called, anyone can join it, whether they’re unionized or not. As long as they obey protocol, workers generally can’t be fired for walking off the job (though they do lose pay). Not so in the US, where “going on strike is a very risky activity”, said Eric Blanc, assistant professor of labor studies at Rutgers and author of the Labor Politics Substack. “If you have to pay rent and make sure your kids have food next week, you’re going to think twice about taking action even if you know it could benefit you.” View image in fullscreen A demonstration in Grenoble in the Isère department in south-eastern France, on 24 October. Photograph: Arnaud Chastagner/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images Still, the US has seen what an effective action can look like, namely the 2018 teachers’ strikes that spread from West Virginia to Kentucky and Arizona. By walking out of their classrooms for more than a week, public school educators “created a crisis” that forced politicians to pay attention, Blanc said, and they did so knowing it would spark anger at either the state or the teachers. To head off the latter outcome, teachers “were really conscious about winning over parents and community members ”, Blanc said. They rallied bus drivers, custodians and other support staff. They coordinated childcare at local community centers and food donations for families affected by missed school meals. The West Virginia strike also “broke with the rules and practice and went straight to the [state] capitol to demand more money”, Blanc noted, ultimately winning a 5% pay raise for all public sector employees in the state. A broad coalition puts power behind the students’ cause So far, the French student protests have drawn a broad coalition without diluting demonstrators’ demands. That owes in part to the unions and activist groups that have piled onto the cause: the gilets jaunes , or yellow vests, a leaderless movement that came together in 2018 to protest fuel-tax increases and eventually the cost of living, set the date for the 17 October action in early September. After the student movement took off, it put out a call on their website inviting “Gen Z, Indignés [anti-austerity activists], farmers, firefighters, workers, teachers, healthcare workers, climate activists, residents of disadvantaged neighborhoods and retirees” to join them. The unions then called for protests on the same day. On 24 October in Paris, the situation went further: multiple groups merged into one march, along one route. “It wasn’t just the numbers that mattered – it’s that we had a single demonstration with everyone,” explained Robi Morder, a jurist and political scientist specializing in student movements. That solidarity is important for the students because it lends legitimacy to a more vulnerable group, and because workers have leverage high schoolers lack. While high school and university students do have their own unions, which represent them in talks with the government, their walkouts don’t have the legal standing that workers’ do. After all, when the lycéens boycott their classes, it “doesn’t bother anyone except the high school students, since stopping work isn’t like in a factory”, Morder said. Teachers’ unions have already organized walkouts in support of the students, and a general strike is coming next week. To get the government’s attention, Morder said, “we have to be very strong and very numerous, that’s the idea: strength in unity”. That idea has taken hold at the local level in the US, too: in Minneapolis this winter, unions, community leaders, mutual aid networks and everyday people pulled together to push back ICE ; and in Cascade Locks, Oregon, voters banded together to recall their elected officials and cancel plans for the construction of a datacenter. Clear, actionable demands Earlier this month, the students drew up a list of 10 emergency measures they’d like to see implemented, including the need for “clean and functional sanitary facilities”, staffed classrooms and buildings adapted to extreme heat and cold. For many workers in France, those complaints are reasonable and relatable. “What’s happening in the high schools is the same situation as in the hospitals and in all the public services,” said Deluermoz. According to Blanc, mobilizing around grievances that are “really widely and deeply felt” tends to be a productive avenue for organizing. “One of the exciting things about the French movement is that it’s focusing on these core issues of economic redistribution,” he said. “It’s oriented not just to making the point, but towards winning something” – which “necessarily obliges a higher degree of sustained participation”. View image in fullscreen More than 35,000 citizens protest in Toulouse, France, on 24 October. Photograph: Alain Pitton/NurPhoto/Getty Images In the US, recent large-scale protests at the national level have often been less about making demands and more about voicing dissent. No Kings, for example, may mobilize parts of the population not previously involved in activism, but its most immediate impact is showing that many people are upset about a certain thing – in this case, authoritarianism. Dana R Fisher, professor and director of the Center for Environment, Community and Equity at American University, said that the US protests generating immediate effects tend to revolve around specific community threats at the state and local levels. Often, these efforts are catalyzed by “a moral shock”, she said: “Someone murdered by ICE, families being targeted at schools by immigration agents.” Successful leveraging of social media More or less since the lycéen movement began, law enforcement has responded with a heavy hand, using military-grade weapons that have cost teenagers eyes, hands and teeth . Online, Deluermoz now sees a “war of images”: protesters and some media have circulated “shocking scenes of police violence inflicted on people under 18, with very childlike faces”. The government has countered by advancing the narrative “of the casseur , of looters, to give the impression of anarchy and justify a use of force that legal experts … consider disproportionate”, Deluermoz said. While photos of shattered Parisian storefronts and Limoges’s flaming city hall may have consumed international headlines, the local story has unfolded a bit differently on social media. The teens have filmed themselves doing viral dances and “aura battles” (a trend in which two people face off in competing displays of charisma) in front of the police. The injection of meme culture into the manifs draws a line under the inherent absurdity of riot police facing off against kids who are asking for more chairs in their classrooms; it also reflects a gen Z-specific sense of humor that translates across borders. Take the now-viral phrase “ bismillah, c’est les ténèbres ”, which entered the lexicon in early October when a screenshot from Snapchat circulated online, apparently showing a request to access an organizer group. “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?” the message said, followed by a string of Algerian flag emojis, according to Al Jazeera . Students quickly blamed undercover cops, reading the nonsensical mashup of Arabic and French slang as an example of racial stereotyping by police. They co-opted the line as a slogan, which has now popped up on protest signs in France as well as Belgium and Italy. While several experts said organizing via social media can prove difficult and ephemeral in the long term, it undeniably catalyzes people to get out into the street. In the US, arguably the clearest example is the Black Lives Matter movement, which sprang from a Facebook post in 2013 after George Zimmerman was acquitted in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin, a Black teenager in Florida, and has leveraged social media as an organizing tool ever since. In May 2020, footage of George Floyd’s murder shared on social media triggered protests against racially motivated police brutality all around the world . In France and now beyond, the footage of young people in the streets has created “solidarity among young people”, as Morder put it. “They recognize each other; they face more or less the same problems.” None of this guarantees the students will get their way – France faces a dire budget crisis and is poised to elect a new president next spring, meaning candidates on both sides of the political spectrum are spinning the protests to serve their own agendas. But the movement has nonetheless surfaced popular concerns that apply not only across France but around the world, putting a point on what people want from their governments. “There’s something deeper at play here,” Morder said. “It’s seeping into society. We see reactions here from adults, parents, grandparents, employees, who say: ‘We’re very proud of the young people, because they’re moving, they’re acting.’” Explore more on these topics Activism Building power France Protest (US) US politics Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
